title: Which Keycloak client holds the power to create users?

title: What happens when the Keycloak call fails after the database commit?

reason: Calling first and committing second can leave a Keycloak user the database has never heard of. Committing first can leave a database row with no identity, which must then be visible and retryable.
suggestions: Commit first, then call Keycloak, and record idp_state (PENDING, SYNCED, FAILED) on the row so an administrator can retry.
Call Keycloak first, then commit.
recommendation: Commit first, then call, with idp_state on the row. A failure then shows up in the admin UI instead of leaving an invisible orphan. This needs a migration with a tested rollback (rule 10).
options: Commit first, then call, with idp_state

question: A failed draft stays a draft. Should repeated failures from one order pause it automatically?
reason: It stops a broken order filling the board.
suggestions: Auto-pause after 3 consecutive quarantined runs and show why.
Leave manual.
recommendation: Auto-pause after 3 consecutive quarantined runs, show why, and let a human resume it.

title: Who really owns each agent?
question: Each contract names an accountable owner role, defaulting to the department head, which is a placeholder. Who owns each agent, and the cross-cutting AI and Security ones?

suggestions: Supply a table of department to role title.
recommendation: Accept the placeholder "Head of <dept>" now and send a table (department to real role title) when you can. I will replace the placeholders from it.

title: Which agents are limited to a reviewed provider?
question: The contract can restrict an agent to named providers but none does. Which agents (legal, finance, security) should be limited to a provider whose terms you have reviewed?
reason: Provider terms differ on retention and training use. That is for you and your attorney; the platform will not assert what any provider's terms say.

title: Who is the attorney, tax adviser and Information Officer?
blocks: Using any of the 65 draft legal documents

title: Which agents need a registered professional or two persons?
question: Beyond legal, should finance, tax, contracts, procurement agents and library policy documents need a registered attorney, accountant or tax practitioner, or two different persons? Who are they, and how are registrations verified? Also confirm how legal artefacts ratified before the change are treated, and whether the ledger should record registration text.
reason: The platform stores registration text but cannot check it. With no OPS_SIGNERS registry nobody holds a profession, so legal artefacts cannot be ratified. A plan conflict was resolved the safe way and needs your confirmation.
suggestions: Register one attorney and a second signer.
Accept that the attorney runs the agent and the owner approves.
recommendation: Register the professionals and a second signer before ratifying any legal artefact, and confirm the safe reading (no grandfathering of earlier legal ratifications). Verification of registrations stays a human step.

Adapt them for dark surfaces.

title: How does the Ecosystem's CI learn that the Ops tokens moved on?
question: Nothing tells the Ecosystem that the Ops brand version changed. (a) A scheduled CI check in the Ecosystem comparing its vendored version with the Ops repo's main (needs read access, so a credential), or (b) a manual check on each Ops brand change?
reason: Without one of these the two copies can diverge unnoticed after brand:sync. Option (a) needs a credential and a cross-repository read.
suggestions: (a) Scheduled CI check with a read credential.
(b) Manual check.
recommendation: (a), the scheduled check. Both repos are public, so the read may not need a credential at all; confirm that before creating one.
